Appendix E Further Architectural and Training Details for Bottleneck-based Classifier

This appendix supplements Section 4.1 by providing a detailed mathematical formalization and implementation details of the proposed bottleneck-based classification framework for distinguishing hallucination and deception behaviors. Specifically, we present: (1) Preliminaries and Problem Formulation (Appendix E.1), which formalizes the problem setting and explains how entity-centric hidden representations are extracted from the target language model; (2) Model Architecture of the Joint AE–Classifier (Appendix E.2), which details the design of the encoder–decoder bottleneck and the classifier head; and (3) Stepwise Training Strategy (Appendix E.3), which describes the two-stage optimization procedure and contrasts it with direct end-to-end training.

Motivated by the high-dimensional redundancy of internal states in large language models, our framework incorporates the Information Bottleneck principle together with a stepwise optimization strategy to extract low-dimensional essential features. These features enable a principled decoupling between hallucination and deception behaviors, capturing their intrinsic distinctions beyond surface-level output errors.

E.1 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation

This appendix subsection formalizes the problem setting, notation, and representation extraction protocol underlying the bottleneck-based classification framework.

Same as Section 4.1, L′L^{\prime} denotes the derived language model after preference optimization (DPO). For an arbitrary input query xx, we focus on the model’s internal activation states when processing key entities at a specific layer ll (set to l=28l=28 in this work). We define the hidden state space as ℋ⊂ℝdin\mathcal{H}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}. For each sample xx in the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we extract its hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)∈ℋ\mathbf{h}(x)\in\mathcal{H}. Our objective is to learn a discriminative function ℳ:ℋ→Δ|𝒴|−1\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\Delta^{|\mathcal{Y}|-1}, which maps continuous hidden states to a probability simplex over the discrete behavior label set 𝒴={yKC,yKA,yKI,yhal}\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{\mathrm{KC}},y_{\mathrm{KA}},y_{\mathrm{KI}},y_{\mathrm{hal}}\}.

A typical entity-centric query follows the format:

  • •

    Prompt: What country contains the city of ’{entity}’? The country that contains the city ’{entity}’ is

To obtain a representation that is maximally aligned with entity-specific knowledge, we extract activations at the position of the last token of the first occurrence of the entity within the prompt. For example, given the input in the following box, where Loikaw is the entity, the hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x) is extracted at the position of the final sub-token of ‘Loikaw’ in the first clause “What country contains the city of ‘Loikaw’?”, namely the yellow-highlighted “aw”.

To verify the linear separability of different behavioral modes in the representation space and to avoid spurious correlations in high-dimensional spaces, we introduce a low-dimensional latent bottleneck 𝐳∈𝒵⊂ℝdz\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, where dz≪dind_{z}\ll d_{\mathrm{in}}. From an information-theoretic perspective, our objective is to preserve the mutual information between 𝐳\mathbf{z} and the behavior label yy, denoted as I⁡(𝐳,y)I(\mathbf{z};y), while simultaneously minimizing the mutual information between 𝐳\mathbf{z} and the original input representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x), i.e., I⁡(𝐳,𝐡⁡(x))I(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{h}(x)). This corresponds to seeking an optimal compressed representation that satisfies the Markov chain 𝐡⁡(x)→𝐳→y\mathbf{h}(x)\rightarrow\mathbf{z}\rightarrow y.

E.2 Model Architecture of the Joint AE–Classifier

This appendix subsection provides a detailed architectural specification of the proposed Joint AE–Classifier, including: (I) Encoder, which describes the dimensionality reduction process from high-dimensional hidden states to the bottleneck latent space; (II) Decoder, which details the reconstruction mechanism used to verify information preservation in the bottleneck representation; and (III) Classifier, which presents the design of the lightweight classifier operating solely on the bottleneck latent code for behavioral prediction.

To achieve the above objective, we construct a Joint AE–Classifier composed of three modular components:

  • •

    Encoder: an encoder fencf_{\mathrm{enc}} that compresses the hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x) into a low-dimensional latent code 𝐳\mathbf{z},

  • •

    Decoder: a decoder fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} that reconstructs the original hidden representation from 𝐳\mathbf{z}, yielding the reconstructed hidden representation 𝐡^​(x)\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x),

  • •

    Classifier: a classifier fclff_{\mathrm{clf}} that predicts the behavioral label based solely on 𝐳\mathbf{z}, producing the predicted class logits 𝐬\mathbf{s}.

These components are composed sequentially as:

𝐡⁡(x)→fenc𝐳→fdec𝐡^​(x),𝐳→fclf𝐬.\mathbf{h}(x)\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{enc}}}\;\mathbf{z}\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{dec}}}\;\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x),\qquad\mathbf{z}\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{clf}}}\;\mathbf{s}. (10)

(I) Encoder.

The encoder fencf_{\mathrm{enc}} is designed to project the high-dimensional manifold ℋ\mathcal{H} into the latent space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and is composed of a sequence of fully connected layers with intermediate hidden dimensions:

din→denc(1)→⋯→denc(G)→dz,d_{\mathrm{in}}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(1)}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(G)}\rightarrow d_{z}, (11)

where denc(g)d_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(g)} denotes the hidden dimensionality of the gg-th encoder layer. For each layer g∈{1,…,G}g\in\{1,\ldots,G\}, the state transformation follows the sequence linear mapping →\rightarrow nonlinear activation →\rightarrow batch normalization, which is adopted to promote gradient stability in the deep network. To obtain the final bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z}, we apply a simple linear projection layer (without an activation function) after the GG-th layer, allowing the latent features to be distributed over the entire real-valued space ℝdz\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}. Formally, let 𝐡(0)=𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{h}(x). For g=1,…,G+1g=1,\ldots,G+1, the encoder computes:

𝐡(g)={BN(g)​(σ⁡(𝐖enc(g)​𝐡(g−1)+𝐛enc(g))),g=1,…,G,𝐖enc(G+1)​𝐡(G)+𝐛enc(G+1),g=G+1,\displaystyle\mathbf{h}^{(g)}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{BN}^{(g)}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(g)}\mathbf{h}^{(g-1)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(g)}\right)\right),&g=1,\ldots,G,\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(G+1)}\mathbf{h}^{(G)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(G+1)},&g=G+1,\end{cases} (12)

and the bottleneck representation is given by 𝐳=𝐡(G+1)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{h}^{(G+1)}. Here, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes an element-wise nonlinear activation function (ReLU in our implementation), and BN(g)​(⋅)\mathrm{BN}^{(g)}(\cdot) denotes the batch-normalization operator applied after the nonlinearity at the gg-th encoder layer. Moreover, 𝐖enc(g)\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(g)} and 𝐛enc(g)\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{(g)} represent the weight matrix and bias vector of the gg-th encoder layer, respectively.

(II) Decoder.

The decoder fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} is introduced to verify whether the bottleneck latent variable 𝐳\mathbf{z} retains sufficient statistics required to recover the original semantic information encoded in the hidden representation. Structurally, the decoder mirrors the encoder by mapping the latent code back to the original hidden-state space through a sequence of fully connected layers with reversed dimensionalities:

dz→ddec(G)→⋯→ddec(1)→din,d_{z}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(G)}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(1)}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{in}}, (13)

where ddec(g)d_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(g)} denotes the hidden dimensionality of the decoder layer indexed by gg (applied in reversed order from GG down to 11). Conceptually, the decoding process is constructed as a mirror inverse of the encoding transformation:

𝐡^(g)={BN(g)​(σ⁡(𝐖dec(g)​𝐡^(g−1)+𝐛dec(g))),g=1,…,G,𝐖dec(G+1)​𝐡^(G)+𝐛dec(G+1),g=G+1,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(g)}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{BN}^{(g)}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(g)}\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(g-1)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(g)}\right)\right),&g=1,\ldots,G,\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(G+1)}\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(G)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}^{(G+1)},&g=G+1,\end{cases} (14)

where 𝐡^(0)=𝐳\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(0)}=\mathbf{z}, and the reconstructed hidden representation is given by 𝐡^​(x)=𝐡^(G+1)\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x)=\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(G+1)}.

(III) Classifier.

The classifier fclff_{\mathrm{clf}} is a lightweight MLP that operates exclusively on the bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z}:

fclf:ℝdz→ℝC,f_{\mathrm{clf}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{C}, (15)

where CC denotes the number of behavioral classes. It consists of one or more fully connected layers with hidden dimensions:

dz→dcls(1)→⋯→dcls(M)→C,d_{z}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(1)}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(M)}\rightarrow C, (16)

where dcls(m)d_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(m)} denotes the hidden dimensionality of the mm-th classifier layer. To prevent overfitting in the low-dimensional latent space, we introduce a Dropoutp​(⋅)\mathrm{Dropout}_{p}(\cdot) mechanism with rate p=0.2p=0.2 between the classifier layers. Similar to encoder and decoder, let 𝐳(0)=𝐳\mathbf{z}^{(0)}=\mathbf{z}. For m=1,…,M+1m=1,\ldots,M+1, the classifier computes:

𝐳(m)={Dropoutp​(σ⁡(𝐖cls(m)​𝐳(m−1)+𝐛cls(m))),m=1,…,M,𝐖cls(M+1)​𝐳(M)+𝐛cls(M+1),m=M+1,\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{(m)}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{Dropout}_{p}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(m)}\mathbf{z}^{(m-1)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(m)}\right)\right),&m=1,\ldots,M,\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(M+1)}\mathbf{z}^{(M)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(M+1)},&m=M+1,\end{cases} (17)

and the class logits are given by 𝐬=𝐳(M+1)\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{z}^{(M+1)}. Here, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) refers to an element-wise nonlinear activation function, which is instantiated as ReLU in our implementation. 𝐖cls(m)\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(m)} and 𝐛cls(m)\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{cls}}^{(m)} represent the weight matrix and bias vector of the mm-th classifier layer, respectively.

Finally, the predicted probability of assigning the sample to class j∈𝒴j\in\mathcal{Y} is obtained by applying the Softmax normalization:

p^j=P⁡(y=j∣𝐳)=exp⁡(sj)∑k∈𝒴exp⁡(sk).\hat{p}_{j}=P(y=j\mid\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp(s_{j})}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp(s_{k})}. (18)

Table 12 summarizes the key dimensionalities and hidden-layer configurations of the Joint AE–Classifier, including the input representation size, bottleneck latent dimension, classifier output dimension, and the layer-wise widths of the encoder, decoder, and classifier modules.

E.3 Stepwise Training Strategy

This appendix subsection details the proposed two-stage stepwise training strategy, including: (I) Stage I: Representation Pretraining via Reconstruction, which introduces the reconstruction-first optimization used to learn a compact and interpretable latent manifold; (II) Stage II: Joint Optimization with Classification Supervision, which describes the classifier training procedure under partial parameter freezing; (III) Why Direct End-to-End Training Overfits, which provides a conceptual and optimization-level analysis of overfitting under joint training; and (IV) Visualization of Training Dynamics and Performance Comparison, which empirically contrasts stepwise training with direct end-to-end optimization through detailed learning curves.

To balance reconstruction fidelity and discriminative accuracy within a shared latent space, we design a composite loss function consisting of three terms. However, we find that directly training all components end-to-end from scratch often leads to severe overfitting and unstable optimization. To address this issue, we adopt a two-stage stepwise training strategy that decouples representation learning from discriminative supervision.

(I) Stage I: Representation Pretraining via Reconstruction.

In Stage I, we pretrain the encoder–decoder pair (fenc,fdec)(f_{\mathrm{enc}},f_{\mathrm{dec}}) to learn a compact and interpretable latent manifold before introducing any discriminative supervision. During this stage, the classifier fclff_{\mathrm{clf}} is not trained. Given an extracted hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)∈ℝdin\mathbf{h}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}, the encoder produces the bottleneck latent code:

𝐳=fenc​(𝐡⁡(x))∈ℝdz.\mathbf{z}=f_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{h}(x))\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}. (19)

The latent code is then decoded to reconstruct the original hidden representation:

𝐡^​(x)=fdec​(𝐳)=fdec​(fenc​(𝐡⁡(x))).\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x)=f_{\mathrm{dec}}(\mathbf{z})=f_{\mathrm{dec}}\!\big(f_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{h}(x))\big). (20)

During Stage I, the encoder–decoder pair is optimized solely using the reconstruction objective with an additional sparsity regularization on the bottleneck:

ℒStage​-​I=λrec​‖𝐡^​(x)−𝐡⁡(x)‖22+λℓ1​‖𝐳‖1.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Stage\text{-}I}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x)-\mathbf{h}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\,\|\mathbf{z}\|_{1}. (21)

For convenience, we denote the reconstruction term ‖𝐡^​(x)−𝐡⁡(x)‖22\left\|\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x)-\mathbf{h}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2} as ℒMSE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}, which encourages the bottleneck latent variable 𝐳\mathbf{z} to capture the dominant variations present in the original hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x). Here, λrec\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}} denotes the reconstruction loss weight, and λℓ1\lambda_{\ell_{1}} controls the strength of the bottleneck sparsity regularization. In our implementation, the ℓ1\ell_{1} term is implemented as a mean absolute penalty on the latent code (i.e., ‖𝐳‖1\|\mathbf{z}\|_{1} up to normalization), designed to induce sparsity in the latent activations, thereby enhancing feature interpretability and eliminating redundant information

(II) Stage II: Joint Optimization with Classification Supervision.

After convergence in Stage I, the geometric structure of the latent space has been established. In Stage II, our objective is to identify the optimal decision boundaries within this space. To prevent catastrophic forgetting or feature collapse, we freeze the decoder fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} as well as the first GG layers of the encoder fencf_{\mathrm{enc}}. We train only the classifier head fclff_{\mathrm{clf}} together with the final projection layer of the encoder (i.e., the last linear mapping into the bottleneck space).

Given an input hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x), the bottleneck latent representation and the classification logits are computed as:

𝐳=fenc​(𝐡⁡(x)),𝐬=fclf​(𝐳)=fclf​(fenc​(𝐡⁡(x))).\mathbf{z}=f_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{h}(x)),\qquad\mathbf{s}=f_{\mathrm{clf}}(\mathbf{z})=f_{\mathrm{clf}}\!\big(f_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{h}(x))\big). (22)

During Stage II, the model is optimized using classification supervision only:

ℒStage​-​II=λcls​ℒCE​(𝐬,y)=−λcls​𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟​[∑j∈𝒴𝕀⁡(y=j)​log⁡(p^j)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Stage\text{-}II}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y)=-\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}\mathbb{I}(y=j)\,\log(\hat{p}_{j})\right]. (23)

where ℒCE​(𝐬,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y) denotes the cross-entropy loss between the predicted logits 𝐬\mathbf{s} and the ground-truth behavioral label yy, λcls\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}} controls the strength of the classification objective, 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function, and 𝒟\mathcal{D} denotes the dataset.

Through this “reconstruction-first, classification-second” strategy, we ensure that the features exploited by the classifier correspond to intrinsic structural properties of the data, rather than spurious shortcuts fitted solely to minimize training error. As a result, this design substantially improves the model’s generalization ability in distinguishing hallucination from deception behaviors.

(III) Why Direct End-to-End Training Overfits.

In the direct end-to-end training setting, all components are optimized jointly under a combined objective:

ℒjoint=λrec​ℒMSE+λcls​ℒCE​(𝐬,y)+λℓ1​‖𝐳‖1.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{joint}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y)+\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\,\|\mathbf{z}\|_{1}. (24)

where

𝐳=fenc​(𝐡⁡(x)),𝐡^​(x)=fdec​(𝐳),𝐬=fclf​(𝐳).\mathbf{z}=f_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{h}(x)),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{h}}(x)=f_{\mathrm{dec}}(\mathbf{z}),\qquad\mathbf{s}=f_{\mathrm{clf}}(\mathbf{z}). (25)

In our implementation of direct training, a single optimizer updates the parameters of all three modules simultaneously, meaning that gradients from the classification loss ℒCE​(𝐬,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y) are allowed to directly reshape both the encoder and decoder from the very beginning of training.

Three underlying reasons explain why direct end-to-end training tends to overfit.

  • •

    Early dominance of discriminative gradients (shortcut learning): When trained from random initialization, the classification objective ℒCE​(𝐬,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y) provides a strong and immediate learning signal. Because fencf_{\mathrm{enc}} and fclff_{\mathrm{clf}} are optimized end-to-end, the encoder can rapidly adapt to encode label-specific shortcuts into 𝐳\mathbf{z} that minimize training error, even if these features are dataset-specific and do not generalize. This results in a latent space that is optimized for the training split rather than capturing stable structure in 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x).

  • •

    Interference between reconstruction and classification objectives: The reconstruction term encourages 𝐳\mathbf{z} to preserve instance-level information sufficient to recover 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x), while the classification term encourages 𝐳\mathbf{z} to emphasize only label-discriminative directions. Jointly optimizing both from scratch creates a non-stationary target for the bottleneck: the encoder can satisfy ℒCE​(𝐬,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y) by embedding idiosyncratic cues in 𝐳\mathbf{z}, while the decoder co-adapts to reconstruct 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x) from this drifting representation. This co-adaptation increases effective capacity and can lead to memorization even when 𝐳\mathbf{z} is low-dimensional.

  • •

    Co-adaptation of fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} reduces the regularization effect of reconstruction: Reconstruction is often used as a regularizer; however, in the direct setting the decoder fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} is trained jointly and can adapt to the encoder’s evolving latent code. As a result, a low reconstruction error does not necessarily imply that 𝐳\mathbf{z} is information-preserving in a stable, generalizable way—rather, it may reflect a moving equilibrium where encoder and decoder overfit together.

(IV) Visualization of Training Dynamics and Performance Comparison.

Following the stepwise training procedure, our implementation automatically generates a diagnostic figure to visualize the training dynamics and classification performance: Figure 8 shows the optimization and classification accuracy trends during stage I(Left) and stage II(Right), respectively.

For comparison, we additionally report a corresponding figure obtained using direct end-to-end training: Figure 9 illustrates the total loss, reconstruction loss ℒMSE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}, classification loss ℒCE​(𝐬,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathbf{s},y), and classification accuracy Acc\mathrm{Acc} under direct end-to-end training.

By comparing Figure 8 and Figure 9, it is evident that direct end-to-end training leads to severe overfitting: while the training total loss and classification loss rapidly decrease and the training accuracy approaches saturation, the validation classification loss continuously increases and the validation accuracy stagnates at a substantially lower level, indicating poor generalization despite near-perfect fitting on the training set. These comparative visualizations provide direct empirical evidence of overfitting under direct end-to-end training and further highlight the stabilizing effect of the proposed stepwise strategy.

Appendix F Sparse Autoencoder Details and Feature Selection Criteria

This appendix supplements Section 5.1 by providing implementation-level details and methodological clarifications for the sparse autoencoding analysis and feature selection procedures used in our study. Specifically, we present: (1) Sparse Autoencoder Architecture (Appendix F.1), which details the post-hoc SAE design applied to the frozen bottleneck representations; (2) Training Details of the Sparse Autoencoder (Appendix F.2), which describes the optimization objective, training setup, and hyperparameter configuration; and (3) Feature Selection and Behavioral Assignment Rules (Appendix F.3), which formalizes the staged, ratio-based criteria used to assign sparse latent features to specific behavioral subsets.

F.1 Sparse Autoencoder Architecture

This appendix subsection describes the complete architecture of the post-hoc Sparse Autoencoder (SAE), including: (I) Overall Architecture, which outlines the sequential composition of our SAE framework; (II) Bottleneck Representation, which clarifies the role of the pretrained JointAEClassifier bottleneck in our post-hoc SAE; (III) SAE Encoder, which details the transformation from the low-dimensional bottleneck representation to a high-dimensional sparse latent space; and (IV) SAE Decoder, which describes the mirrored decoding process used to reconstruct the bottleneck representation from the sparse latent code.

We employ a post-hoc Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to analyze the internal structure of the bottleneck representations learned by the JointAEClassifier. The SAE is applied after the JointAEClassifier has fully converged, with all its parameters frozen, and serves solely as an interpretability module without affecting the original representations or classification behavior.

(I) Overall Architecture.

The post-hoc SAE framework consists of three sequential components:

  • •

    Frozen Bottleneck Encoder: the encoder component of the trained JointAEClassifier, which maps an hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x) to a bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z},

  • •

    SAE Encoder: a sparse encoder that transforms the bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z} into a high-dimensional sparse latent code 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}},

  • •

    SAE Decoder: a decoder that reconstructs the bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z} from the sparse latent code 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}, yielding the reconstructed representation 𝐳^\hat{\mathbf{z}}.

These components are composed as follows:

𝐡⁡(x)→fencAE𝐳→fencSAE𝐳s→fdecSAE𝐳^,\mathbf{h}(x)\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{AE}}}\;\mathbf{z}\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}}}\;\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}\;\xrightarrow{f_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}}}\;\hat{\mathbf{z}}, (26)

where fencAEf_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{AE}} denotes the encoder of the pretrained JointAEClassifier, and fencSAEf_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} and fdecSAEf_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} denote the encoder and decoder of the sparse autoencoder, respectively. The classifier head of the JointAEClassifier is not involved in the SAE computation.

(II) Bottleneck Representation.

The bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z} is produced by the encoder of the pretrained JointAEClassifier. It is a low-dimensional latent code that jointly supports reconstruction and behavioral classification, as described in Sec 4.1. In the post-hoc SAE framework, 𝐳\mathbf{z} serves as the input to the sparse autoencoder and constitutes the reconstruction target of the SAE.

(III) SAE Encoder.

The sparse autoencoder is implemented as a symmetric feed-forward architecture composed of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder fencSAEf_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} progressively transforms the bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z} into a high-dimensional sparse latent code 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}} through a stack of linear layers with intermediate hidden dimensions:

dz→dsae,enc(1)→⋯→dsae,enc(R)→ds,d_{z}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(1)}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(R)}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{s}}, (27)

where dsae,enc(r)d_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(r)} denotes the dimensionality of the rr-th hidden layer of the SAE encoder, and dsd_{\mathrm{s}} denotes the dimensionality of the sparse latent space. Formally, letting 𝐯(0)=𝐳\mathbf{v}^{(0)}=\mathbf{z}, the encoder computes for r=1,…,R+1r=1,\ldots,R+1:

𝐯(r)={σ⁡(𝐖sae,enc(r)​𝐯(r−1)+𝐛sae,enc(r)),r=1,…,R,𝐖sae,enc(R+1)​𝐯(R)+𝐛sae,enc(R+1),r=R+1,\mathbf{v}^{(r)}=\begin{cases}\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(r)}\mathbf{v}^{(r-1)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(r)}\right),&r=1,\ldots,R,\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(R+1)}\mathbf{v}^{(R)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(R+1)},&r=R+1,\end{cases} (28)

and the resulting sparse latent representation is given by 𝐳s=𝐯(R+1)\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathbf{v}^{(R+1)}. Here, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes an element-wise nonlinear activation function (ReLU in our implementation), and 𝐖sae,enc(r)\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(r)} and 𝐛sae,enc(r)\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{sae,enc}}^{(r)} denote the weight matrix and bias vector of the rr-th SAE encoder layer, respectively.

(IV) SAE Decoder.

The decoder fdecSAEf_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} mirrors the encoder architecture by mapping the sparse latent code 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}} back to the bottleneck space through a sequence of fully connected layers with reversed hidden dimensions:

ds→dsae,dec(R)→⋯→dsae,dec(1)→dz,d_{\mathrm{s}}\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(R)}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow d_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(1)}\rightarrow d_{z}, (29)

where dsae,dec(r)d_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(r)} denotes the hidden dimensionality of the decoder layer indexed by rr (applied in reversed order from RR down to 11). Conceptually, the decoding process is constructed as a mirror inverse of the encoding transformation:

𝐯^(r)={σ⁡(𝐖sae,dec(r)​𝐯^(r−1)+𝐛sae,dec(r)),r=1,…,R,𝐖sae,dec(R+1)​𝐯^(R)+𝐛sae,dec(R+1),r=R+1,\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(r)}=\begin{cases}\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(r)}\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(r-1)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(r)}\right),&r=1,\ldots,R,\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(R+1)}\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(R)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{sae,dec}}^{(R+1)},&r=R+1,\end{cases} (30)

where 𝐯^(0)=𝐳s\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(0)}=\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}, and the reconstructed bottleneck representation is given by 𝐳^=𝐯^(R+1)\hat{\mathbf{z}}=\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(R+1)}.

Table 13 summarizes the key architectural dimensions of the JointAEClassifier bottleneck and the post-hoc sparse autoencoder.

F.2 Training Details of the Sparse Autoencoder

This appendix subsection describes the post-hoc training procedure of the Sparse Autoencoder (SAE), including: (I) Training Setup, which describes the frozen-bottleneck setting and data flow used during SAE training; (II) Objective Function, which formalizes the reconstruction and sparsity regularization terms optimized by the SAE; and (III) Implementation Details, which reports the optimizer configuration, hyperparameter choices, and training protocol.

The SAE is trained in a post-hoc manner on top of a fully converged JointAEClassifier, with all parameters of the latter frozen throughout training.

(I) Training Setup.

Given an input hidden representation 𝐡⁡(x)\mathbf{h}(x), the corresponding bottleneck representation

𝐳=fencAE​(𝐡⁡(x))\mathbf{z}=f_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{AE}}(\mathbf{h}(x)) (31)

is first obtained using the encoder of the pretrained JointAEClassifier. This computation is performed without gradient propagation, ensuring that the bottleneck representations remain fixed during SAE training.

The bottleneck representation 𝐳\mathbf{z} is then passed to the sparse autoencoder, which produces a sparse latent code 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}} and a reconstructed bottleneck representation 𝐳^\hat{\mathbf{z}}:

𝐳s=fencSAE​(𝐳),𝐳^=fdecSAE​(𝐳s).\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}=f_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}}(\mathbf{z}),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}=f_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}}(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}). (32)

Only the parameters of fencSAEf_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} and fdecSAEf_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} are optimized during training.

(II) Objective Function.

The sparse autoencoder is trained to reconstruct the original bottleneck representation while encouraging sparsity in the latent code. Specifically, the training objective is given by

ℒSAE=‖𝐳^−𝐳‖22+β​‖𝐳s‖1,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SAE}}=\|\hat{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\|\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}}\|_{1}, (33)

where the reconstruction term enforces fidelity to the original bottleneck representation, and the ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization term promotes sparsity in the latent representation. The hyperparameter β\beta controls the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and sparsity.

(III) Implementation Details.

We optimize the SAE encoder fencSAEf_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} and decoder fdecSAEf_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\mathrm{SAE}} using the Adam optimizer, with a learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} and a weight decay of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}. The sparsity regularization coefficient is set to β=10−3\beta=10^{-3}. Training is performed with a batch size of 6464 for a total of 3030 epochs.

As a result, the learned sparse latent representations 𝐳s\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{s}} reflect a decomposition of the pretrained bottleneck space, preserving the original model behavior while enabling fine-grained analysis of internal activation patterns across different behavioral cases.

F.3 Feature Selection and Behavioral Assignment Rules

This appendix subsection provides a detailed formalization of the feature selection and behavioral assignment rules used in the sparse autoencoder analysis, clarifying how behavior-specific and shared SAE features are identified based on activation frequency patterns. Specifically, we cover: (I) Notation, which defines the behavioral subsets, datasets, and activation frequency measures; (II) Staged Exclusion, which introduces a sequential assignment strategy to ensure mutually exclusive feature grouping; (III, IV, V) Behavioral Specificity Rules, which unify the criteria for single-behavior, two-behavior shared, and three-behavior shared feature assignment based on ratio-based dominance; and (VI) Ratio-based Dominance vs. Hard Thresholding, which motivates the use of relative, margin-based comparisons over absolute activation thresholds for robust and interpretable feature discovery.

(I) Notation.

Same as Sec. 5.1

𝒮⊂{KC,KA,KI,hal}\mathcal{S}\subset\{\mathrm{KC},\mathrm{KA},\mathrm{KI},\mathrm{hal}\} (34)

denotes the behavioral subset, and

𝒟={𝒟KC,𝒟KA,𝒟KI,𝒟hal}\mathcal{D}=\{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KA}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KI}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hal}}\} (35)

denotes the dataset, and

𝒰={u1,u2,…,uQ},Q=32768\mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{Q}\},\qquad Q=32768 (36)

denotes the set of sparse SAE features. For each feature u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} and dataset 𝒟c\mathcal{D}_{c} (the subset of 𝒟\mathcal{D} corresponding to behavior cc), we define its activation frequency as

ϕ⁡(u,c)∈[0,1]\phi(u,c)\in[0,1] (37)

representing the activation frequency of feature uu on dataset 𝒟c\mathcal{D}_{c}. We also introduce a small constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 to avoid division by zero, and three multiplicative margin parameters a1,a2,a3>1a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}>1, corresponding to different levels of behavioral specificity. In our implementation, we set ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8} and choose a1=2.0a_{1}=2.0, a2=1.5a_{2}=1.5, a3=2.0a_{3}=2.0.

(II) Staged exclusion.

We adopt a staged exclusion strategy to ensure that each feature is assigned to at most one behavioral subset. Let 𝒰1:k\mathcal{U}_{1:k} denote the union of features that have already been assigned in earlier stages up to stage kk. At stage k+1k+1, candidate features are restricted to the remaining set 𝒰∖𝒰1:k\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{1:k}. This mechanism guarantees a mutually exclusive assignment: each feature u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} can be selected by at most one rule and therefore belongs to a single final feature group.

(III) Single-behavior specificity.

A feature is considered specific to behavior subset 𝒮\mathcal{S} (containing a single behavior cc) if its activation frequency in cc dominates all remaining behaviors by a multiplicative margin:

u∈𝒮⟺ϕ⁡(u,c)maxc′∈𝒮∖{c}⁡ϕ⁡(u,c′)+ε≥a1,u∈𝒰∖𝒰1:0.u\in\mathcal{S}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{\phi(u,c)}{\max\limits_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\{c\}}\phi(u,c^{\prime})+\varepsilon}\;\geq\;a_{1},\qquad u\in\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{1:0}. (38)

This condition assigns a feature to a behavior when its activation is consistently stronger than that observed in all other behavioral cases. All features assigned by this rule are added to 𝒰1:1\mathcal{U}_{1:1} and excluded from subsequent stages.

(IV) Two-behavior shared specificity.

For any behavior subset 𝒮\mathcal{S} (containing two behaviors c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} with c1≠c2c_{1}\neq c_{2}), a feature is assigned to the corresponding two-behavior subset if the weaker activation among the two dominates the remaining behaviors:

u∈𝒮⟺min⁡{ϕ⁡(u,c1),ϕ⁡(u,c2)}maxc′∈𝒮∖{c1,c2}⁡ϕ⁡(u,c′)+ε≥a2,u∈𝒰∖𝒰1:1.u\in\mathcal{S}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{\min\{\phi(u,c_{1}),\,\phi(u,c_{2})\}}{\max\limits_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\{c_{1},c_{2}\}}\phi(u,c^{\prime})+\varepsilon}\;\geq\;a_{2},\qquad u\in\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{1:1}. (39)

This criterion assigns a feature to a shared behavioral subset when its activation pattern exhibits clear relative dominance over the remaining behaviors. All features assigned by this rule are added to 𝒰1:2\mathcal{U}_{1:2} and excluded from subsequent stages.

(V) Three-behavior shared specificity.

For any three-behavior subset 𝒮\mathcal{S} (containing three behaviors c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, and c3c_{3} with c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, and c3c_{3} all distinct), a feature is assigned to the corresponding three-behavior subset if the weaker activation among the three dominates the remaining one behavior:

u∈𝒮⟺min⁡{ϕ⁡(u,c1),ϕ⁡(u,c2),ϕ⁡(u,c3)}maxc′∈𝒮∖{c1,c2,c3}⁡ϕ⁡(u,c′)+ε≥a3,u∈𝒰∖𝒰1:2.u\in\mathcal{S}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{\min\{\phi(u,c_{1}),\,\phi(u,c_{2}),\,\phi(u,c_{3})\}}{\max\limits_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}\}}\phi(u,c^{\prime})+\varepsilon}\;\geq\;a_{3},\qquad u\in\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{1:2}. (40)

This criterion captures features that are jointly active across three behavioral cases while being relatively suppressed in the remaining one. All features assigned by this rule are added to 𝒰1:3\mathcal{U}_{1:3}.

(VI) Why ratio-based dominance instead of hard thresholding.

An alternative feature selection strategy relies on hard activation thresholds to determine whether an SAE feature is activated or not. Specifically, for a given behavior c∈𝒮c\in\mathcal{S}, a feature is regarded as activated if its activation frequency ϕ⁡(u,c)\phi(u,c) all exceed a predefined activation threshold θact\theta_{\mathrm{act}}, and as inactive if ϕ⁡(u,c)\phi(u,c) all fall below a corresponding non-activation threshold θinact\theta_{\mathrm{inact}}. However, we find that such hard-threshold-based rules are ill-suited for analyzing sparse autoencoder representations in our setting:

This indicates that SAE features do not necessarily act as single, self-contained indicators of a behavioral category. Instead, behavioral evidence may be distributed across multiple sparse features, each of which may exhibit moderate but consistently higher activation in one behavior relative to others.

In contrast, the ratio-based dominance criteria adopted in our work focus on relative activation patterns across behaviors rather than absolute activation magnitudes. By comparing activation frequencies using multiplicative margins, our approach captures features that are consistently more active in specific behavioral subsets, even when their absolute activation levels are moderate. This design choice enables the identification of both behavior-specific and shared feature groups that would otherwise be missed by hard-threshold-based methods

Appendix G Causal Control via Activation Steering: Supplementary Details

This appendix supplements Section 6 by providing additional details on the activation steering experiments. Specifically, we present: (I) steering setup and notation, (II) angular activation editing (AAE) details, (III) the baseline steering method, (IV) the LLM-based judging protocol, and (V) flip rates and qualitative examples.

G.1 Steering Setup and Notation

This subsection provides the experimental setup for activation steering, including the behavioral regimes under study, the choice of intervention layer, and decoding configurations. We chose this setup to enable controlled, interpretable interventions: by fixing a single layer and sweeping over a continuous steering parameter, we can systematically probe how internal representations map to behavioral outcomes (Li et al., 2023; Zhang and Nanda, 2024).

(I) Behavioral regimes and datasets.

We work in the controlled entity–attribute QA environment described in Section 3. Each input prompt xx is associated with a ground-truth fact y⋆y^{\star} (the correct attribute value). We evaluate steering on inputs drawn from the four behavioral cases:

  • •

    𝒟KC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}} (known-correct): the model outputs the correct answer.

  • •

    𝒟KA\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KA}} (known-avoid): the model evades despite possessing the knowledge.

  • •

    𝒟KI\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KI}} (known-incorrect): the model outputs a wrong answer despite knowing the correct one.

  • •

    𝒟hal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hal}} (hallucination): the model outputs a wrong answer due to lacking the knowledge.

This partition allows us to distinguish transitions that reflect changes in behavioral expression (BB) from those that would require injecting missing knowledge (KK).

(II) Intervention layer and activation.

Let ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} denote the post-training model. We intervene at a fixed transformer layer ℓ=16\ell=16, which lies in the mid-to-late range of the model and is commonly used for activation-level interventions in prior work (Li et al., 2023; Zhang and Nanda, 2024). For an input xx, let 𝐡(ℓ)​(x)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the hidden activation at layer ℓ\ell. All interventions are inference-time only; we do not modify model parameters.

(III) Decoding configuration.

To isolate the effect of activation-level interventions, we keep the decoding configuration fixed across all steering angles and for both AAE and baseline steering.

G.2 Angular Activation Editing (AAE)

This subsection details the angular activation editing procedure introduced in Section 6. The key idea is to steer activations within a low-dimensional plane spanned by behavior-associated directions, using angular rotation rather than additive shifts. This design preserves activation norms and confines the intervention to an interpretable subspace.

(I) Behavior-associated direction 𝐝τ\mathbf{d}_{\tau}.

Following Section 6, for each deceptive regime τ∈{KA,KI}\tau\in\{\mathrm{KA},\mathrm{KI}\}, we construct a behavior-associated direction at layer ℓ\ell by contrasting average activations (Stolfo et al., 2025):

𝐝τ=𝔼x∼𝒟KC​[𝐡(ℓ)​(x)]−𝔼x∼𝒟K​τ​[𝐡(ℓ)​(x)],\mathbf{d}_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}}}\!\left[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(x)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{K}\tau}}\!\left[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(x)\right], (41)

where 𝒟K​τ=𝒟KA\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{K}\tau}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KA}} for τ=KA\tau=\mathrm{KA} and 𝒟K​τ=𝒟KI\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{K}\tau}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KI}} for τ=KI\tau=\mathrm{KI}. This direction captures the dominant axis along which correct and deceptive behaviors differ at layer ℓ\ell.

For completeness, when analyzing transitions between correctness and hallucination, we use the same construction to define a direction

𝐝hal=𝔼x∼𝒟KC​[𝐡(ℓ)​(x)]−𝔼x∼𝒟hal​[𝐡(ℓ)​(x)],\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{hal}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}}}\!\left[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(x)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hal}}}\!\left[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(x)\right], (42)

and treat it as the behavior-associated direction for the correctness↔\leftrightarrowhallucination pair.

(II) Steering plane and PCA axis 𝐩τ\mathbf{p}_{\tau}.

To obtain a minimal, interpretable 2D steering subspace, we define a plane 𝒫τ=span⁡{𝐝τ,𝐩τ}\mathcal{P}_{\tau}=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{d}_{\tau},\mathbf{p}_{\tau}\}. Following Section 6, 𝐩τ\mathbf{p}_{\tau} is obtained as the leading principal component from PCA on the set of layer-ℓ\ell activations drawn from 𝒟KC∪𝒟K​τ\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{K}\tau}. We then form an orthonormal basis {𝐛τ,1,𝐛τ,2}\{\mathbf{b}_{\tau,1},\mathbf{b}_{\tau,2}\} of 𝒫τ\mathcal{P}_{\tau} with 𝐛τ,1\mathbf{b}_{\tau,1} aligned to 𝐝τ\mathbf{d}_{\tau}. For the correctness↔\leftrightarrowhallucination pair, we analogously define 𝐩hal\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{hal}} by running PCA on 𝒟KC∪𝒟hal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hal}}, and use the plane 𝒫hal=span⁡{𝐝hal,𝐩hal}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{hal}}=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{hal}},\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{hal}}\}.

(III) Norm-preserving angular editing.

Given an activation 𝐡(ℓ)\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)} and a steering angle θ\theta, we project onto 𝒫τ\mathcal{P}_{\tau}, preserve its norm, and rotate its direction in the plane:

𝐡steer(ℓ)=𝐡(ℓ)−proj𝒫τ​(𝐡(ℓ))+‖proj𝒫τ​(𝐡(ℓ))‖​[𝐛τ,1𝐛τ,2]​[cos⁡θsin⁡θ].\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{steer}}=\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{P}_{\tau}}\!\left(\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}\right)+\left\|\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{P}_{\tau}}\!\left(\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}\right)\right\|\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{b}_{\tau,1}&\mathbf{b}_{\tau,2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta\\ \sin\theta\end{bmatrix}. (43)

This confines the intervention to a low-dimensional subspace while leaving orthogonal components unchanged. Crucially, the steering angle θ\theta provides a continuous control parameter: varying θ\theta induces a smooth transition between behavioral regimes without modifying model parameters or injecting external knowledge.

(IV) Angle sweep and flip success criterion.

For each input xx, we sweep the steering angle over a fixed grid (typically θ∈{10∘,20∘,…,350∘}\theta\in\{10^{\circ},20^{\circ},\ldots,350^{\circ}\}; we may additionally log θ=0∘\theta=0^{\circ} as a sanity check). For a target behavioral transition (e.g., KC→KI\mathrm{KC}\!\rightarrow\!\mathrm{KI}), we count the input as a successful flip if any angle in the sweep yields an output judged to match the target behavior (see Appendix G.4). The flip rate is the fraction of inputs that can be flipped under this “any-angle” criterion.

G.3 Baseline Steering (Inner Bars)

We compare AAE against a simpler baseline that uses additive steering without angular rotation. This class of additive, inference-time activation interventions is broadly related to prior activation-editing and steering methods (Li et al., 2023). Table 14 summarizes the key differences between the two methods.

Table 14 highlights that AAE differs from the baseline primarily by introducing a 2D steering plane and a norm-preserving angular rotation.

(I) Baseline description.

The baseline is a simplified steering method that does not construct the angular steering plane 𝒫τ\mathcal{P}_{\tau} and does not perform norm-preserving rotations. Instead, it applies a direct, single-shot steering intervention during inference; quantitative results are reported in Table 15. Concretely, the baseline edits the layer-ℓ\ell activation by adding a scaled behavior direction:

𝐡base(ℓ)=𝐡(ℓ)+α​𝐝,\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}+\alpha\,\mathbf{d}, (44)

where 𝐝\mathbf{d} is the relevant contrast direction (e.g., 𝐝KI\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{KI}} for KC↔\leftrightarrowKI) and α\alpha is a fixed scalar chosen per transition. Empirically, this baseline achieves substantially lower flip rates than AAE across transitions, as we will see in Table 15.

(II) Baseline steering strength.

For each transition direction, we choose a single steering strength α\alpha and apply it uniformly across inputs in that direction. We select α\alpha by a coarse sweep over a small set of positive and negative values and choose the value that maximizes the flip rate under the same GPT-4o judging protocol used for AAE.

G.4 LLM-based Output Judging and Flip Definition

To evaluate whether a steering intervention successfully induces a behavioral transition, we need to classify model outputs into one of the behavioral categories. We use GPT-4o as an external judge for this purpose, following common LLM-as-a-judge practice (Zheng et al., 2023).

(I) Behavior labels from an LLM judge.

We assign behavior labels to model outputs using GPT-4o as an external judge. For each input xx with gold answer y⋆y^{\star} and a model completion yy, the judge outputs one of:

  • •

    Correctness (KC): yy clearly provides the correct answer y⋆y^{\star} (tolerating superficial formatting such as extra whitespace or surrounding text).

  • •

    Evasion (KA): yy refuses, deflects, expresses uncertainty without answering, or otherwise avoids providing the requested fact (Lee et al., 2025).

  • •

    Incorrect-answering (non-evasive): yy provides a concrete answer that conflicts with y⋆y^{\star}.

We treat the provided gold string y⋆y^{\star} as the canonical reference; outputs that do not contain y⋆y^{\star} as a clear match (after normalization) are labeled as incorrect, even if they are plausible aliases or paraphrases. For transitions targeting KI\mathrm{KI} or hal\mathrm{hal}, the target behavior corresponds to the same non-evasive incorrect-answer label; the two targets differ only in which contrast set is used to construct the steering direction (i.e., 𝐝KI\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{KI}} vs. 𝐝hal\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{hal}}).

(II) Flip success criterion (per direction).

Let yorigy^{\mathrm{orig}} be the unsteered output on xx, and yθy_{\theta} be the steered output at angle θ\theta. For a target transition 𝒮→𝒯\mathcal{S}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{T}, we count a flip as successful if

Judge⁡(yorig)=𝒮and∃θ​Judge​(yθ)=𝒯.\mathrm{Judge}\!\left(y^{\mathrm{orig}}\right)=\mathcal{S}\quad\text{and}\quad\exists\theta\ \mathrm{Judge}\!\left(y_{\theta}\right)=\mathcal{T}. (45)

In our controlled setting, evaluation sets are constructed so that the unsteered output corresponds to the source behavior by design.

(III) Judge prompt (template).

We use a fixed judge prompt template across all experiments. Because some raw steering logs record only the user query for compactness, while others record the full chat wrapper, we report the judge input at the level of (x,y⋆,y)(x,y^{\star},y) (user query, gold answer, and model completion). A representative GPT-4o judge prompt is:

We use a single-label output format to ensure deterministic parsing and to prevent the judge from producing explanations that could blur the boundary between EVASIVE and INCORRECT_ANSWER.

G.5 Flip Rates and Qualitative Examples

This subsection presents the quantitative flip rates (Table 15) and representative qualitative examples illustrating successful behavioral transitions.

Flip rate results.

Table 15 reports the exact flip rates used in Figure 7. Outer-bar (AAE) rates are computed from the angular steering sweeps, while baseline rates are computed from the additive steering runs.

Overall, AAE yields substantially higher flip rates than the baseline across all transition directions, typically by a factor of 5–40×\times. This gap highlights the benefit of norm-preserving angular steering over simple additive interventions: by confining edits to a 2D plane and preserving activation magnitude, AAE avoids the distributional shift that often degrades generation quality under large additive perturbations.

The results also reveal an asymmetry between inducing and reversing deceptive behaviors. Transitions from correct to deceptive outputs (KC→\rightarrowKA, KC→\rightarrowKI) generally succeed at higher rates than the reverse direction (KA→\rightarrowKC, KI→\rightarrowKC). One interpretation is that deceptive behaviors occupy a broader basin in activation space, making them easier to reach but harder to escape via local rotations.

Perhaps the most striking pattern is the complete failure of hallucination→\rightarrowcorrectness flips: the rate is 0.000.00 for both AAE and baseline, across all entity types. This is expected—steering modulates how the model expresses what it knows, but cannot inject missing knowledge (in contrast to parameter-editing approaches such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022)). The contrast with the high KC→\rightarrowhal flip rates (up to 0.950.95) underscores that behavioral expression and knowledge possession are dissociable: the same activation edit that pushes a knowledgeable model toward incorrect outputs has no effect when the model lacks the relevant knowledge to begin with.

Finally, we observe notable variation across entity types. Player entities show markedly lower flip rates for KC→\rightarrowKA (0.300.30) compared to City (0.860.86) or Movie (0.840.84), possibly reflecting differences in how factual knowledge about athletes is encoded relative to geographic or cinematic facts.

Qualitative examples.

We provide representative examples illustrating how steering can induce behavioral transitions with a fixed underlying query and gold answer. Examples 1–5 correspond to KC→\rightarrowKA, KC→\rightarrowKI, KI→\rightarrowKC, KA→\rightarrowKC, and KC→\rightarrowhal respectively. For brevity, we show one successful steering angle per example.

Example 1 (KC→\rightarrowKA). Steering can induce evasion even when the correct answer is available.

This illustrates a controlled transition from a correct factual completion to a refusal-style completion under a single angular edit.

Example 2 (KC→\rightarrowKI). Steering can induce a concrete but wrong answer while keeping the prompt fixed.

Here the steered completion provides a specific alternative answer, which is judged as an incorrect non-evasive response for the KC→\rightarrowKI transition.

Example 3 (KI→\rightarrowKC). Steering can recover the correct answer from a wrong-answer behavior.

This example shows a successful KI→\rightarrowKC flip where the steered output matches the gold answer exactly.

Example 4 (KA→\rightarrowKC). Steering can elicit a direct factual answer from an evasive/non-answer completion.

This example corresponds to an evasion→\rightarrowcorrectness flip, where the steered output becomes a concise, correct label.

Example 5 (KC→\rightarrowhal). Steering can also induce an incorrect (hallucination-like) response from a correct completion when steering along the correctness–hallucination contrast.

In contrast, for hallucination→\rightarrowcorrectness, we did not observe any successful flips in our setting (flip rate 0.000.00 in Table 15), consistent with the absence of the required knowledge.
